source.title: Neutrino-nucleus interactions: open questions and future projects

accepted.question_text: How can the unknown quantity L1,A in neutrino-deuteron reaction theory be determined, and how would determining L1,A improve the precision of calculations relevant to the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory deuteron detector response and to the solar proton-proton reaction?

evidence.quote: The best known case is the neutrino-deuteron reaction, relevant for the SNO experiment [16], where theoretical calculations reach the few percent precision [17]. However, there is still an important unknown quantity L1,A whose determination would improve our knowledge of the pp reaction in the Sun.

accepted.question_text: What explains and resolves the remaining discrepancy between experiment and theory for neutrino interactions on carbon, especially for neutrinos produced from the decay-in-flight of pions, despite several years of theoretical and experimental effort?

evidence.quote: The most studied case, namely neutrino interactions on carbon, still suffer from a discrepancy between experiment and theory, in particular for the neutrinos produced from the decay-in-flight of pions, in spite of the efforts done during several years [18].

accepted.question_text: What are the precise neutrino-oxygen reaction cross sections in the several-hundred-MeV energy range needed for next-generation Megaton neutrino detectors such as Hyper-K or UNO, particularly when those detectors are used to study CP violation in the lepton sector?
accepted.context_brief: Oxygen cross sections for Megaton detectors

evidence.quote: A precise measurement of the reactions on oxygen is of great interest also in view of the next-generation experiments involving Megaton detectors like Hyper-K or UNO [19]. In particular, their use with the aim of studying CP violation in the lepton sector would need a very precise determination of the reaction cross sections in the range of several hundred MeV.

accepted.question_text: What are the precise differential cross sections of electrons emitted in charged-current neutrino interactions on lead, and can such measurements provide reliable information about neutrino temperatures at emission if a core-collapse supernova occurs?

evidence.quote: Lead represent an interesting nucleus as well, e.g. for supernova observatories [20,21,22,23,24]. In this context, the precise measurement of the differential cross sections of electrons emitted in charge-current events would be very useful, since their measurement would give us precious information on the neutrino temperatures at emission, if a core-collapse supernova explodes [23].

accepted.question_text: What experimental information can be obtained about the nuclear excited states probed by neutrinos in the charged-current 208Pb(νe, e−)208B reaction, especially states with multipolarities Jπ = 0−, 1−, and 2− for which little information is available and higher-multipolarity states for which no information is available?
accepted.context_brief: Neutrino probes of poorly known nuclear excited states

evidence.quote: In particular, neutrinos can be used to perform nuclear structure studies since neutrinos probe nuclear excited states for which little or no experimental information is available (Figure 1) [22].
Note that little experimental information is available on the Jπ=0−, 1−, 2− states and none on those having higher multipolarity.

accepted.question_text: How can a larger set of experimental neutrino-nucleus data strengthen the interpolation between low-energy neutrino-nucleus models, such as Elementary Particle Theory, Effective Field Theories, the shell model, and the Random-Phase Approximation, and high-energy descriptions based on the Fermi Gas, while also improving extrapolations to neutron-rich nuclei of astrophysical interest that are not experimentally accessible?

evidence.quote: While the description of the low-energy regime exploits approaches like the Elementary Particle Theory, Effective Field Theories, or microscopic models, such as the shell model or the Random-Phase-Approximation, the Fermi Gas is the basis for the theoretical description in the high energy regime.

A larger ensemble of experimental data would put the interpolation, of the neutrino-nucleus interaction modeling between these two regimes, on even more solid grounds. This would also help the extrapolation to the case of neutron-rich nuclei of astrophysical interest that are not experimentally accessible.

accepted.question_text: Which low-energy neutrino-beam facility strategy can provide the intense beams needed to address open neutrino-nucleus interaction questions: a conventional source based on pion and muon decay, or a beta-beam source based on accelerated beta-decaying nuclei that produces pure electron-neutrino or electron-antineutrino beams with tunable mean energy Eν ≃ 2γQβ?

evidence.quote: In order to address these (and other) open questions, one needs a facility producing intense low-energy neutrinos.
There are essentially two options for a facility producing low-energy neutrino beams: either a conventional one, based on the decay of pions and muons, or beta-beams [28].
Conventional sources provide us with neutrinos of different flavours, while beta-beams produce pure electron neutrino (or anti-neutrino) beams.
Beta-beams have the specific feature that the neutrino mean energy depends on the ion acceleration according to Eν ≃ 2γQβ, where γ is the Lorentz gamma factor and Qβ is the beta-decay Q-value.

accepted.question_text: Can a low-energy beta-beam facility, either at a future exotic-ion laboratory such as GSI, GANIL, EURISOL, or RIA or as part of the high-energy CERN beta-beam facility, meet the essential requirements of attainable ion intensity and an available storage ring for ions?

evidence.quote: Two possible scenarios can be envisaged for a low-energy beta-beam facility [28] where it is part either of one of the future nuclear laboratories (or projects) for the production very intense exotic ion beams (like e.g. GSI, GANIL, EURISOL or RIA), or of the high energy beta-beam facility at CERN.
For the former case, there are several requirements which should be met. Two essential aspects are the ion intensity which can be attained and the availability of a ring to store the ions.

accepted.question_text: After realistic detector-response simulations and background modeling, what final neutrino-nucleus interaction event rates would be obtained at a low-energy beta-beam facility for target nuclei such as deuteron, oxygen, iron, and lead, given that preliminary rates assume 100% efficiency and realistic ion intensities from feasibility studies?

evidence.quote: Note that the rates shown are obtained by considering realistic ion intensities, namely 2 × 1013 ¯ν/s (from 6He decay) and 8 × 1011 ν/s (from 18Ne decay), as obtained in the first feasibility study [34]. An efficiency of 100% is considered for all cases. Final rates will be given by detailed simulations of the detector response taking into account possible backgrounds.
Neutrino-nucleus interaction rates (events/year) at a low-energy beta-beam facility [38]: Rates on deuteron, oxygen, iron and lead are shown as examples.

accepted.question_text: Can a low-energy beta-beam source at rest, combined with very low-threshold detectors and accurately calculated neutrino fluxes, improve current direct limits on the neutrino magnetic moment by almost an order of magnitude, and what precise sensitivity remains after detailed detector-response simulation?
accepted.context_brief: Low-energy beta-beam sensitivity to neutrino magnetic moment

evidence.quote: To improve present direct limits on the neutrino magnetic moment one needs : i) very intense neutrino sources of well-known fluxes; ii) very low threshold detectors.
Clearly in this case - as for a static source [45,46,47] - the neutrino fluxes can be very accurately calculated.
This indicates that the present direct limits might be improved by almost an order of magnitude, the precise value requiring a detailed simulation of the detector response.

accepted.question_text: For low-energy beta-beam applications, can ion production rates higher than those obtained in the first feasibility study be achieved for at least one beta-beam emitter?

evidence.quote: For these low energy applications it would be of great interest to investigate if, at least for one beta-beam emitter, higher ion production rates, than the ones obtained in the first feasibility study, can be achieved.
